title: Pandas DataFrames, Selection and Transformation
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Pandas DataFrames, Selection and Transformation.
Use the relevant NumPy or pandas APIs to solve a data task.
Inspect shapes, labels, dtypes and missing-value behaviour.
Choose appropriate operations and validate their outputs.
Identify performance, correctness and data-quality limitations.

understand.concept: A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure with rows and columns. Each column is a Series and may have its own dtype. DataFrames support selection, filtering, column creation, sorting and aggregation. A DataFrame is useful for rectangular datasets, but it does not automatically guarantee clean types, unique identifiers or valid business rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Data analysis depends on choosing correct representations and operations. Understanding these structures helps learners process datasets accurately and explain their results.
understand.analogy: A DataFrame resembles a table with named columns and indexed rows. Unlike a static spreadsheet, it is a Python object whose operations can return new objects or modify existing data depending on the method and assignment.
understand.summary: Pandas DataFrames, Selection and Transformation adds practical library skills to the Python data-analysis workflow.

explain.narrative: Create a DataFrame from dictionaries, lists or arrays. Select a column with df['column'], select rows by label with .loc and by position with .iloc. Use boolean masks for filtering, assign a new column explicitly and sort with sort_values(). Avoid chained assignment; select and assign in a single .loc operation. Inspect dtypes and shape after transformations.

examples.title: Create a DataFrame
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
data = {'item': ['Pen', 'Book'], 'qty': [3, 2]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df['item'].tolist())
examples.explanation: A dictionary of equal-length columns creates a tabular DataFrame.

examples.title: Inspect shape
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'score': [70, 80, 90]})
print(df.shape)
examples.explanation: shape reports the number of rows and columns.

examples.title: Select by condition
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['A', 'B'], 'score': [55, 82]})
print(df.loc[df['score'] >= 60, 'name'].tolist())
examples.explanation: loc combines a row condition with a selected column.

examples.title: Add a derived column
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'price': [10, 20], 'qty': [2, 3]})
df['total'] = df['price'] * df['qty']
print(df['total'].tolist())
examples.explanation: A vectorized expression derives one total per row.

examples.title: Sort rows
examples.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['B', 'A'], 'score': [70, 90]})
ordered = df.sort_values('score', ascending=False)
print(ordered['name'].tolist())
examples.explanation: sort_values orders records by a selected column and returns a sorted DataFrame.

practise.guidedTask: Create an orders DataFrame with item, quantity and unit price. Add a total column, filter orders above a minimum and sort by total descending.
practise.independentTask: Build a small student-results DataFrame. Select rows using multiple conditions, add a pass/fail column and explain the difference between .loc and .iloc.
hints: All columns used to construct a DataFrame should have compatible lengths.
Avoid chained assignment; assign through df.loc[...] or a new DataFrame.
practise.challenge: Write a function that validates required columns and returns a new sorted DataFrame without mutating the caller's input.
